paragraphs: The Caterpillar and Alice looked at each other in silence for some time. At last the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth and spoke to her in a languid, sleepy voice.
“Who are you?” said the Caterpillar.

This was not an encouraging way to start a conversation. Alice replied rather shyly, “I—I hardly know, sir, just at the moment. At least I know who I was when I got up this morning, but I think I must have been changed several times since then.”
“What do you mean by that?” said the Caterpillar sternly. “Explain yourself!”
“I’m afraid I can’t explain myself, sir,” said Alice, “because I’m not myself, you see.”
“I don’t see,” said the Caterpillar.
“I’m afraid I can’t put it any more clearly,” Alice replied very politely, “because I can’t understand it myself, to begin with. And being so many different sizes in one day is very confusing.”
“It isn’t,” said the Caterpillar.

“Well, maybe you haven’t found it so yet,” said Alice. “But when you have to turn into a chrysalis (and you will someday, you know) and then after that into a butterfly, I think you’ll find it a little strange, won’t you?”
“Not a bit,” said the Caterpillar.
“Well, maybe your feelings are different,” said Alice. “All I know is that it would feel very strange to me.”
“You!” said the Caterpillar contemptuously. “Who are you?”

Which brought them back to the beginning of the conversation. Alice felt a little irritated by the Caterpillar’s very short remarks. She drew herself up and said, very seriously, “I think you ought to tell me who you are first.”
“Why?” said the Caterpillar.
Here was another puzzling question, and since Alice couldn’t think of a good reason, and the Caterpillar seemed to be in a very unpleasant mood, she turned away.
“Come back!” the Caterpillar called after her. “I have something important to say!”
This sounded promising, at least. Alice turned and came back.
“Keep your temper,” said the Caterpillar.
“Is that all?” said Alice, swallowing her anger as well as she could.
“No,” said the Caterpillar.

Alice thought she might as well wait, since she had nothing else to do, and perhaps it would tell her something worth hearing after all. For some minutes it puffed away without speaking, but at last it unfolded its arms, took the hookah out of its mouth again, and said, “So you think you’ve changed, do you?”
“I’m afraid I have, sir,” said Alice. “I can’t remember things the way I used to, and I don’t stay the same size for ten minutes at a time!”
“Can’t remember what things?” said the Caterpillar.
“Well, I tried to recite ‘How Doth the Little Busy Bee,’ but it all came out different!” Alice replied in a very gloomy voice.
“Recite ‘You Are Old, Father William,’” said the Caterpillar.
Alice folded her hands and began:
“You are old, Father William,” the young man said, “And your hair has become very white; And yet you keep standing on your head— Do you think, at your age, that’s right?”
“In my youth,” Father William replied to his son, “I feared it might injure my brain; But now that I’m perfectly sure I have none, Why, I do it again and again.”
“You are old,” said the youth, “as I mentioned before, And have grown most uncommonly fat; Yet you turned a backflip in through the door— Please, what’s the reason for that?”
“In my youth,” said the sage, as he shook his gray locks, “I kept all my limbs very supple By the use of this ointment (one shilling the box)— May I sell you a couple?”
“You are old,” said the youth, “and your jaws are too weak For anything tougher than fat; Yet you finished the goose, with the bones and the beak— Please, how did you manage that?”
“In my youth,” said his father, “I took to the law, And argued each case with my wife; And the muscular strength which it gave to my jaw Has lasted the rest of my life.”
“You are old,” said the youth, “one would hardly suppose That your eye was as steady as ever; Yet you balanced an eel on the end of your nose— What made you so awfully clever?”
“I have answered three questions, and that is enough,” Said his father. “Don’t give yourself airs! Do you think I can listen all day to such stuff? Be off, or I’ll kick you downstairs!”
“That’s not right,” said the Caterpillar.
“Not quite right, I’m afraid,” said Alice timidly. “Some of the words got changed.”
“It’s wrong from beginning to end,” said the Caterpillar firmly, and there was silence for a few minutes.
The Caterpillar was the first to speak.
“What size do you want to be?” it asked.
“Oh, I’m not particular about size,” Alice replied hastily. “It’s just that one doesn’t like changing so often, you know.”
“I don’t know,” said the Caterpillar.
Alice said nothing. She had never been contradicted so much in her life, and she felt she was losing her temper.
“Are you happy now?” said the Caterpillar.
“Well, I’d like to be a little bigger, sir, if you wouldn’t mind,” said Alice. “Three inches is such a wretched height to be.”
“It’s a very good height indeed!” said the Caterpillar angrily, rearing itself upright as it spoke (it was exactly three inches tall).
“But I’m not used to it!” pleaded poor Alice in a pitiful tone. And she thought to herself, “I wish these creatures weren’t so easily offended!”
“You’ll get used to it in time,” said the Caterpillar, and it put the hookah back in its mouth and began smoking again.

This time Alice waited patiently until it chose to speak again. In a minute or two the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth, yawned once or twice, and shook itself. Then it climbed down off the mushroom and crawled away into the grass, merely remarking as it went, “One side will make you grow taller, and the other side will make you grow shorter.”
“One side of what? The other side of what?” Alice thought to herself.
“Of the mushroom,” said the Caterpillar, just as if she had asked out loud, and a moment later it was out of sight.

Alice stood thoughtfully looking at the mushroom for a minute, trying to work out which were its two sides. Since it was perfectly round, she found this a very difficult question. However, at last she stretched her arms around it as far as they would go and broke off a bit of the edge with each hand.
“Now, which is which?” she said to herself, and she nibbled a little of the right-hand piece to see what would happen. The next moment she felt a violent blow under her chin: it had hit her foot!

She was quite frightened by this very sudden change, but she knew there was no time to lose, since she was shrinking rapidly. So she set to work at once to eat some of the other piece. Her chin was pressed so tightly against her foot that there was hardly room to open her mouth, but she managed it at last and swallowed a bit of the left-hand piece.

“There, my head is free at last!” said Alice in a tone of delight, which turned to alarm a moment later when she found that her shoulders were nowhere to be found. All she could see when she looked down was an immense length of neck, which seemed to rise like a stalk out of a sea of green leaves far below her.

“What can all that green stuff be?” said Alice. “And where have my shoulders gone? And oh, my poor hands, how come I can’t see you?” She was moving them around as she spoke, but nothing seemed to happen except a little shaking among the distant green leaves.

Since there seemed no chance of getting her hands up to her head, she tried to get her head down to them, and was delighted to find that her neck could bend easily in any direction, like a snake. She had just succeeded in curving it down into a graceful zigzag and was about to dive in among the leaves, which she discovered were just the tops of the trees she had been wandering under, when a sharp hiss made her pull back in a hurry. A large pigeon had flown into her face and was beating her violently with its wings.
“Serpent!” screamed the Pigeon.
“I’m not a serpent!” said Alice indignantly. “Leave me alone!”
“Serpent, I say again!” repeated the Pigeon, but in a more subdued tone, and it added with a kind of sob, “I’ve tried everything, and nothing seems to suit them!”
“I have no idea what you’re talking about,” said Alice.
“I’ve tried the roots of trees, and I’ve tried banks, and I’ve tried hedges,” the Pigeon went on, without paying attention to her. “But those serpents! There’s no pleasing them!”
Alice was more and more puzzled, but she thought there was no point in saying anything until the Pigeon had finished.
“As if it weren’t trouble enough hatching the eggs,” said the Pigeon. “But I also have to watch out for serpents night and day! Why, I haven’t had a wink of sleep in three weeks!”
“I’m very sorry you’ve been bothered,” said Alice, who was beginning to see what it meant.

“And just when I’d taken the highest tree in the woods,” continued the Pigeon, raising its voice to a shriek, “and just when I thought I’d finally be free of them, they have to come wriggling down from the sky! Ugh, serpent!”
“But I’m not a serpent, I tell you!” said Alice. “I’m a—I’m a—”
“Well! What are you?” said the Pigeon. “I can see you’re trying to make something up!”
“I—I’m a little girl,” said Alice, rather doubtfully, remembering how many changes she had gone through that day.

“A likely story!” said the Pigeon in a tone of the deepest contempt. “I’ve seen plenty of little girls in my time, but never one with a neck like that! No, no! You’re a serpent, and there’s no use denying it. I suppose you’ll tell me next that you’ve never tasted an egg!”
“I have tasted eggs, certainly,” said Alice, who was a very truthful child. “But little girls eat eggs just as much as serpents do, you know.”
“I don’t believe it,” said the Pigeon. “But if they do, then they’re a kind of serpent, that’s all I can say.”

This was such a new idea to Alice that she was silent for a minute or two, which gave the Pigeon a chance to add, “You’re looking for eggs, I know that well enough, and what does it matter to me whether you’re a little girl or a serpent?”
“It matters a great deal to me,” said Alice hastily. “But I’m not looking for eggs, as it happens, and if I were, I wouldn’t want yours. I don’t like them raw.”

“Well, be off, then!” said the Pigeon in a sulky tone, settling back down into its nest. Alice crouched down among the trees as well as she could, because her neck kept getting tangled in the branches, and every now and then she had to stop and untwist it. After a while she remembered that she was still holding the pieces of mushroom in her hands, and she set to work very carefully, nibbling first at one and then at the other, growing sometimes taller and sometimes shorter, until she had managed to bring herself down to her usual height.

It was so long since she had been anywhere near the right size that it felt quite strange at first, but she got used to it in a few minutes and began talking to herself as usual. “Well, that’s half my plan done! How puzzling all these changes are! I’m never sure what I’m going to be from one minute to the next! Still, I’m back to my right size. The next thing is to get into that beautiful garden. How am I going to do that, I wonder?” As she said this, she suddenly came upon an open space with a little house in it, about four feet high. “Whoever lives there,” thought Alice, “it won’t do to meet them at this size. Why, I’d frighten them out of their wits!” So she began nibbling at the right-hand piece again, and didn’t dare go near the house until she had brought herself down to nine inches tall.
